doc.title: Jackie Cain and Roy Kral interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

chapter: Studio notes, hits and old friends
title: The new 'East of Suez' arrangement for Concord
summary: Carl Jefferson asks for 'East of Suez' for a Concord album; the song's origin as a Lou Stein tune for Ventura.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Tell me about “East of Suez” and how that was conceived. Is the arrangement that you did on—

This is a new arrangement of “East of Suez.” Because the original was not in our key, it was something that Charlie had down and that’s the way he kept it. And we were out of our range, we’d have to keep jumping octaves and stuff. So Jeff from Concord, Jeff the owner—
Oh, I can’t think of his name right now, yeah.
I can’t remember. He heard us do it at a concert.
Carl Jefferson. He said, “you’ve got to do that song as part of a new CD you’re going to do for me, a new album you’re going to do for me.”
He loved it, he loved it.
And so we did, but I had to change the key and do the whole thing over. And different instrumentation.

That was actually a Lou Stein tune that he had written for Charlie and Charlie did it with Buddy Stewart and Kai Winding. And it was recorded that way the first time, but then when we joined the band he wanted us to do it naturally, because it was a good record for him, a big record. So that’s how we started doing it. But we love it. I think it’s a great piece.
This particular arrangement reminds me of like how I usually hear “Green Dolphin Street” with the Latin and swing, back and forth. It’s a nice exchange.
Yeah. That’s another popular jazz, people always ask for that. We’ve never done it, but maybe one of these days.
